summary:
Ondo is a state in south-western Nigeria and stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the secular criminal provisions covering same-sex conduct extend to Ondo in full, and the sources record no Ondo statute, protective measure or enforcement divergence of the state's own. Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria does not name Ondo at all.

The Shari'a penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can carry death by stoning, are separate jurisdictions; the maximum penalty recorded for the southern portion of the country is a life sentence, and the exposure in Ondo is the secular framework, including up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions under the 2014 act.

Ondo also sits under section 217 of the Criminal Code, quoted in the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025: any male who commits or procures an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or in private, is guilty of a felony and liable to three years' imprisonment. The Code does not define the act. Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, recorded in a January 2017 book chapter that the provision fails to state what constitutes gross indecency, so the boundary of the offence is not set out in the statute.

No legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection and no recognition of same-sex relationships is recorded for Ondo. The Home Office note documents the national framework applying across all states, including countrywide patterns of arrest, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people, and records no Ondo-specific divergence in either direction.

No Ondo-specific arrest, raid, prosecution or violent incident appears in the sources. The countrywide harm patterns are not broken down by state, so this record does not establish how often the framework is enforced in Ondo or by which agency.
tangentialFactors:
The Shari'a death-penalty layer that draws much of the external travel advice on Nigeria operates in twelve northern states and is absent from Ondo. A visitor's exposure here is the secular three-year felony under section 217 together with the 2014 act's 14-year maximum, not capital punishment.

The definitional gap in section 217 is documented from within Ondo itself. A senior law lecturer at Adekunle Ajasin University published the critique in a January 2017 book chapter, and the sources record no later amendment supplying a definition.

Documentation of Ondo is thin. The principal online overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria does not mention the state, and no state assembly statute, police directive or court decision specific to Ondo appears in the inventory. That leaves enforcement practice in Ondo unmeasured rather than absent.
localsOnly:
Ondo residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no legal recognition of gender identity is recorded for the state. A resident in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no legal recognition, and conduct connected to it falls under the 2014 act as it extends to Ondo, with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Enforcement exposure for male residents includes section 217 of the Criminal Code, a felony carrying three years' imprisonment for an act of gross indecency with another male in public or in private, with the act itself left undefined in the statute.

Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state is the institution whose law faculty documented that gap in January 2017.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether section 217 has been charged or prosecuted in Ondo is not sourced. The inventory contains no Ondo case law, arrest record or prosecution figure.

The Wikipedia overview carrying the findings that there is no recognition of gender identity and no anti-discrimination protection is undated in the inventory, so the currency of those negatives is unresolved.

Ayeni's critique dates from a January 2017 book chapter. Whether the Criminal Code has since been amended to define gross indecency, or whether Ondo's authorities apply a working definition in practice, is unresolved in these sources.

No Ondo-based support organisation, legal-aid scheme or police liaison arrangement for LGBT+ residents appears in the inventory. This is an absence of sourcing, not a finding that none exists.

Whether Ondo's police or correctional services have documented screening or placement practice for transgender detainees is not sourced here.
